title: How I got highlighted by OpenAI in their pretraining competition
description: Two small ideas: share vocabulary across capitalization, and let learning survive the end of a document.
markdown:
OpenAI [highlighted my CaseOps tokenizer](https://openai.com/index/what-parameter-golf-taught-us/) in its Parameter Golf write-up. It started with a simple question: why should a tiny language model spend vocabulary entries learning that “apple,” “Apple,” and “APPLE” are related?

[Parameter Golf](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf) gave us **16 MB for the model artifact, ten minutes to train on eight H100s, and ten minutes to evaluate**. The score was bits per byte on held-out text: how many bits the model needed to predict each byte. Lower was better.

I worked on **CaseOps**, a tokenizer that shares vocabulary across capitalization patterns, and **phased test-time training**, which carries learning from one evaluation document into the next.

## CaseOps: learn the word once

A case-sensitive tokenizer can give “apple,” “Apple,” and “APPLE” different vocabulary entries or different subword splits. With only 8,192 entries, that duplication is expensive.

CaseOps separates spelling from capitalization:

<!--CASEOPS_SHARING-->

The same lowercase pieces work in all three cases. Capitalization becomes a reusable operation the model can apply to any word.

<!--CASEOPS_DEMO-->

The implementation is small: transform the text before BPE tokenization, then undo the transform when decoding. Title case and all caps each need one operator. Mixed case uses an operator that capitalizes the next letter; an escape operator handles literal control characters. Non-ASCII characters pass through unchanged.

The transformer itself doesn't change. We're giving it a representation where related words already share their spelling, instead of asking it to discover that relationship from scratch.

### The detail that makes the score meaningful

Adding capitalization operators changes the length of the encoded text. If we divided the loss by that new byte count, we could make the score look better just by making the representation longer.

So the exporter saves **original byte counts alongside the tokens**. The evaluator divides by those counts. The model pays to predict every capitalization operator, and the denominator still measures the text we started with.

My [submission](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1729) combined CaseOps with a late weight-decay taper on the existing phased-TTT stack: **1.06780 bits per byte**, averaged over three seeds, in **15.94 MB**, a new record. The [code and tokenizer details are here](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/tree/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-18_PR1626_CaseOps_Taper).

## Phased TTT: let learning survive the document

The competition allowed the model to learn from text **after scoring it**, to help predict what came next. Earlier scores stayed fixed.

[Samacqua's evaluator](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1530) already used that within each document: score a chunk, train a small LoRA adapter on it, then predict the next chunk. At the document boundary, reset the adapter.

That gives the model a useful short-term memory. But every new document starts from the same base model. My addition was a second, slower learning loop: **update the base model using completed documents, so later documents inherit what it learned.**

<!--TTT_DIAGRAM-->

My [first implementation](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1610) paused after 2,000 completed documents, ran distributed SGD on that already-scored prefix, then resumed evaluation. Each new document still got a fresh local adapter, now on top of an improved base.

### Why pause instead of learning continuously?

I first tried mixing local and global updates more continuously. Synchronizing the shared model across GPUs kept getting in the way of the local work.

Phases made the coordination simple: **score in parallel, pause for a shared training phase, then go back to scoring**. It also makes the information flow obvious. Global training only sees documents whose scores are already recorded.

With pretraining unchanged, the [three-seed mean](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/blob/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-13_VarLenAttn_PhasingTTT2000/README.md) improved from **1.07336 → 1.07281 bits per byte**, a new record, while staying within the evaluation time limit.

[Dexhunter extended it to three phases](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1626), and I built CaseOps on top of that version. Every later record built on both CaseOps and phased TTT.

title: Reverse engineering DiMuon through a training API
description: A hidden optimizer, a programmable LoRA adapter, and a symmetry trick that made the update rule fall out.
markdown:
Thinking Machines released DiMuon, a LoRA optimizer available through [Tinker](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/optimizers/), without publishing its update equations. I tried to recover them using only the API.

I ended up with a local reconstruction that replayed **four batches of SST2 gradients with every recovered FP16 polar-output value matching**. That experiment used rank-one LoRA on Qwen3-8B's output projection, with gradients measured at Tinker's weights.

## The rule: scale, polar, scale again

[Muon](https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/) takes a momentum matrix and approximately makes its nonzero singular values equal. This stops the largest singular direction from dominating the update.

The interesting addition in DiMuon is a **row-and-column sandwich**. The previous momentum determines which rows and columns to scale. Apply that scaling before Muon's polar transform, then apply it again afterward.

<!--DIMUON_SANDWICH-->

Rows and columns with stronger old momentum get smaller multipliers. The two LoRA matrices—the wide A and tall B—get the same final update norm.

The scaling statistics are cheap to compute from the momentum the optimizer already keeps.

## The trick: turn the model into a linear system

LoRA learns a weight change **BA**: A compresses an input into a few coordinates, and B expands it back out. The original model weight stays frozen.

At initialization, **B = 0**. Put that adapter on the output projection, and the transformer supplies a fixed feature h. The trainable addition to the logits is just sBAh. From B's perspective, an eight-billion-parameter language model has become a linear system.

The loss simplifies too. Cross-entropy contains a shared log-sum-exp term; signed token weights that sum to zero cancel it. What's left is a linear combination of logits.

Now I could construct useful gradient patterns instead of hoping ordinary text would produce them. To read those gradients back, I borrowed [Martin Marek's large-epsilon Adam trick](https://x.com/mrtnm/status/2114145574987702525): choose an invertible optimizer step, download the weights, and undo the step mathematically. Adam became my gradient meter.

## Making the unknown cancel

I wanted to know whether DiMuon scaled the matrix **after** the polar transform. But I hadn't reproduced that transform precisely yet.

So I chose a gradient that made two axes equal at its input. Symmetry forces the polar computation to treat them equally. Their common response cancels when you take the output ratio—leaving the post-scaling exposed.

<!--DIMUON_ISOLATION-->

The predicted ratio agreed with the API to about eight significant figures.

A second simple experiment explained where the scaling came from: build history with learning rate zero, then set beta to zero for the measured step. The current momentum forgets the past, yet the update still changes. The old momentum is doing a second job: choosing the row and column scaling.

## Same math, different program

The numerics turned into a second puzzle: **which way of computing the same equation matched the API?** Three details stood out.

### Rearrange the polynomial

Each polar stage applies a polynomial to the working matrix X. Here R = XᵀX, I is the identity, and a, b, c are that stage's coefficients. I initially evaluated it in expanded form. Switching to **Horner form** made the difference:

<!--DIMUON_HORNER-->

The coefficients stayed the same. The rearranged version matched all eleven of my retained numerical fingerprints.

This is a natural optimization for LoRA: X is tall and skinny, while R is only rank × rank. Folding the aX term into the small matrix avoids a separate multiply-and-add over the entire large matrix. It also changes where rounding happens. The algebra alone doesn't tell you which program ran.

### Catch an intermediate being rounded

Inside the Horner calculation, **cR gets rounded to FP16 before adding bI**. Keeping that intermediate in higher precision gives a different answer.

I made two inputs specifically to distinguish those implementations. Skipping the FP16 store missed their tiny output ratios by about **20% and 4.6%**; including it matched both to roughly **4 × 10⁻⁸** relative error.

That's a surprisingly specific thing to learn through an API. A low-precision tensor operation naturally leaves this kind of trace: the result gets stored before the next operation reads it. “More accurate” arithmetic erased the trace I was trying to reproduce.

### Let the GPU split up the work

One CPU replay still differed by **0.79%**. Native FP16 matrix products on an H100 brought that case to roughly **8 × 10⁻⁸**. The first Gram matrix differed by just one FP16 rounding step; the polynomial amplified it.

Profiling my GPU replay exposed a useful reason: **split-K**. The GPU divides a long dot product into chunks, computes them in parallel, then combines the partial sums. That helps keep it busy when the output matrix is tiny—exactly the shape LoRA produces. [cuBLAS allows those partial sums to be stored in FP16](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.8.0/cublas/index.html#cublasltreduction-scheme-t), adding another rounding boundary.

<!--DIMUON_SPLITK-->

I could reproduce two of my GPU execution paths by changing only the split count and partial-sum precision. That parallelization choice left a visible signature in the optimizer's output.

[Run the four-step replay on GitHub](https://github.com/romeerp/dimuon-replay) · [Update equations and experiment details →](/reverse-engineering-dimuon/notes/) · [Replay data →](/data/dimuon-replay-2026-10-31.json)
notes:
These are the equations and measurement details behind [Reverse engineering DiMuon through a training API](/reverse-engineering-dimuon/).

## The gradient-meter equations

With no clipping or weight decay, a coordinate moves by:

```math
u=-\eta\frac{g}{|g|+\epsilon},
\qquad
g=-\frac{\epsilon u}{\eta-|u|}.
```

Large epsilon avoids saturation. I repeated measurements with different epsilon values to check the recovered gradients, including their rounding.

## The complete update equations

After optional joint gradient clipping, form the current momentum:

```math
M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\widetilde G_t.
```

Compute energies from the previous momentum:

```math
e_i=\sum_j M_{t-1,ij}^2,
\qquad f_j=\sum_i M_{t-1,ij}^2.
```

Normalize each vector by its maximum, add a small ridge, and take the inverse fourth root:

```math
D_r=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{e_i}{\max_k e_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right],
```

```math
D_c=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{f_j}{\max_k f_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right].
```

Zero old momentum uses relative energies of one. The ridge keeps inactive coordinates from getting unbounded multipliers. Energy is a squared norm, so its inverse fourth root is an inverse square root of the norm.

Then:

```math
U_t=D_r\,\Phi(D_rM_tD_c)\,D_c,
\qquad \Delta\theta_t=-\eta C(r)\frac{U_t}{\|U_t\|_F}.
```

Φ includes the approximate polar computation and its input normalization. A zero direction gets a zero update. At alpha 32, tested ranks 1 through 64 followed:

```math
C(r)=\sqrt r\left(\frac r{32}\right)^{0.175}.
```

This predicted a held-out rank-16 norm to about 5.6 × 10⁻⁸ relative error. The origin of 0.175 is still a mystery.

## The polar computation I replayed

Normalize the preconditioned momentum and store it in FP16:

```math
X=\operatorname{round}_{\mathrm{FP16}}\left(
\frac{D_rM_tD_c}{1.01\max(\|D_rM_tD_c\|_F,10^{-7})}
\right).
```

For a tall matrix, form the small Gram matrix R = XᵀX and apply a stage:

```math
X\leftarrow X\left[aI+R(bI+cR)\right].
```

The coefficients change each stage. Wide matrices use the transposed construction. The intermediate stores matter, as does how the GPU reduces each matrix product.

## Experiment and measurement details

The ordinary steps use learning rate 0.001. Subtracting two nearly equal exported weights loses precision, so I also measure updates with the learning rate enlarged to 16. That changes the readout gain while keeping the optimizer state and gradient fixed.

With that readout, relative update errors were 7.6 × 10⁻⁸ to 1.21 × 10⁻⁷. At the ordinary learning rate, errors in the subtracted updates range from roughly 2 × 10⁻⁶ to 2.4 × 10⁻⁵; the accumulated local weights differ from the hosted weights by at most 9.3 × 10⁻¹⁰. The replay uses measured gradients at the hosted weights; it does not recompute them with a separate local language model. Other experiments include an unresolved 0.81% discrepancy in a rank-two B continuation and 1.14% RMS across historical A updates. The [replay data](/data/dimuon-replay-2026-10-31.json) covers the four-step rank-one experiment.

title: Two NanoGPT experiments: attention gradients and table votes
description: Skipping some attention backward work, and letting an n-gram table vote on the answer.
markdown:
On the [modded-nanogpt](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt) short track, the goal is to get below 3.28 validation loss as fast as possible. Here are two things I tried, and both set records when I submitted them. The table-vote run is the current record, pending the official leaderboard update. In one run I let an attention head look further back than I was willing to backpropagate. In the other I gave a lookup table a vote on the next token, even though the model had already seen its hints.

## A shorter backward pass

Say a head puts almost all its attention on the last few tokens. In the forward pass it still has to score the distant tokens to find out how much they matter. By the time we go backward, though, we already know where the attention went. How much work would we save by skipping the distant tokens for that head?

<!--NANO_ATTENTION-->

In [my run](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/371), I picked the window by trying it. On steps 592 and 593 I ran backward with windows of 64, 128, and 256 tokens, then compared each head's query, key, and value gradients with the full-window gradients. If all three came within 20% relative L2 error on both steps and every GPU, that window was good enough. Each eligible head got the cheapest window that passed. A head that needed the whole window kept it.

The nice part is that nothing changes about what the model reads. Even in backward, the nearby tokens keep the attention weights they got when they competed with *all* the tokens. The kernel just skips the distant tiles.

I also cut down the work on the output layer. For its weight gradient, I sampled one token row in four from the dense positive terms and multiplied its contribution by four. I kept the target-token corrections and the gradient flowing back into the model in full. With both changes on the same eight H100s, average training time went from **40.34 to 39.58 seconds**. The last 87 updates used the regular backward pass.

## Give the table a vote

[Herman Brunborg's run](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/367) brought training time down from about 40 seconds to 6.7. While the GPUs trained the transformer, the CPUs built a lookup table from 37 billion training tokens. If the last few tokens of a passage looked familiar, the table could tell the transformer what usually came next.

The model gets those hints during training. But 540 updates isn't much time to learn how seriously to take a match. So I tried something that sounds a little silly: give the transformer the hint, let it make its prediction, then ask the *same table* for its opinion again.

In [the table-vote run](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/399), each matching continuation gets one vote. The model gets `k` votes to split among tokens according to its probabilities. Add up the votes and divide by the total. A miss leaves the prediction alone.

<!--NANO_VOTE-->

I do this for matches of length 6, then 10, then 20, feeding each result into the next vote. I picked `k` on a training shard outside the table. For a six-token match the model gets about 707 votes; for ten tokens it gets 43; for twenty it gets fewer than three. So a handful of repeats can move the prediction quite a bit if they agree for twenty tokens first.

I used 526 updates and built the table from 36.1 billion tokens. With those same trained weights, switching the vote on took mean validation loss from **3.2933 to 3.2737** across seven seeds. Without the vote, every seed missed 3.28. With it, all seven cleared it.

title: KL is the wrong ruler for quantized models
description: KL measures how different two models' predictions are. Accuracy depends on the mistakes the quantized model actually makes.
markdown:
Quantizing a language model stores its weights in fewer bits, which makes it cheaper to run and slightly worse at everything. How much worse? Running a full evaluation after every change is slow and expensive, so most people use a faster check: the **KL divergence** between the quantized model and the original.

It usually works. But [Applied Compute noticed](https://www.appliedcompute.com/research/making-quantized-models-more-accurate) that when you *train* a quantized model to recover accuracy, KL can fall while accuracy doesn't. I ran into the same thing and wanted to understand why, and what to measure instead.

The short version: KL measures how different the two models' *predictions* are on the original model's text. What actually costs accuracy is the quantized model making *mistakes* on its own solutions. Those turn out to be quite different things, and a simple count of the second one tracks accuracy better than KL.

## Background: a language model as a decision-maker

It helps to look at a language model the way reinforcement learning looks at an agent.

When a model solves a math problem, it writes one token at a time. At each step it sees everything written so far (the **state**) and picks the next token (the **action**) from a probability distribution. A complete solution is a sequence of these choices, and at the end we check the answer: the **reward** is 1 if it's right and 0 if it's wrong. Accuracy is the average reward.

A quantized model is the same decision-maker with slightly perturbed probabilities. Call the original model *p* and the quantized one *q*.

**KL divergence** measures how different two probability distributions are. At one position, if the original model gives "7" probability 0.99 and the quantized model gives it 0.9, KL is small. If the quantized model gives it 0.001, KL is large. The usual damage score averages this over every position of some text, normally text written by the original model.

To talk about which choices matter, we need two more ideas:

- **Value:** the chance that the original model, continuing from a given state, ends with the right answer.
- **Advantage** of a token: how much choosing that token changes the value. Writing "Let's" instead of "We" usually changes nothing: advantage near zero. Writing the wrong digit in the middle of a calculation can drop the chance of a correct answer from 90% to 0%: a large negative advantage.

A classic result from reinforcement learning, the [performance difference lemma](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~pabbeel/cs287-fa09/readings/KakadeLangford-icml2002.pdf), says exactly how much accuracy one model loses relative to another:

```math
\text{acc}(q) - \text{acc}(p) = \mathbb{E}_{\text{solutions written by } q}\Big[\sum_t A_p(\text{state}_t, \text{token}_t)\Big]
```

In words: follow the quantized model as it writes its own solutions. At each token, ask how much that token changed the original model's chance of getting the answer right. Add those up, and on average you get exactly the change in accuracy. Tokens that hurt count as negative, so a quantized model that keeps picking harmful tokens ends up with a large negative total.

Two things about this formula matter for everything that follows. It's computed on the **quantized model's own solutions**, not the original model's. And it only counts tokens that **change the outcome**. KL does neither.

## The puzzle

I quantized Qwen3-8B in many ways and measured accuracy on 1,819 grade-school and competition math problems. Some checkpoints used plain **post-training quantization** (PTQ): round the weights and stop. Others used **quantization-aware distillation** (QAD): after rounding, train the quantized model to imitate the original, usually by minimizing KL. Altogether I made 45 checkpoints.

KL often put them in the wrong order:

- **Same KL, different accuracy.** One PTQ format and one QAD checkpoint both had KL ≈ 0.013. The PTQ model lost **0.5** points of accuracy; the QAD model lost **1.9**.
- **Different KL, same accuracy.** Two QAD checkpoints trained with different losses lost the same accuracy, but one had 3× the KL of the other.
- **KL falls while accuracy falls.** Halfway through one QAD run, the model had *half* the KL of the model it started from but *lower* accuracy.

Within one kind of checkpoint, say a set of PTQ formats, KL does reasonably well. It breaks when you compare checkpoints made in different ways, which is exactly the comparison you need when deciding between recipes.

## The hypothesis: a weighted KL

The lemma suggests what's wrong. KL treats every position the same, but accuracy only depends on positions where the choice changes the outcome. So my starting hypothesis was that we need a **weighted KL**: count divergence where tokens matter and ignore it where they don't.

The ideal weight is the advantage itself, but computing it means running many continuations from every position, which costs far more than an evaluation. We need a cheap stand-in. So which positions matter?

To find out, I took solutions written by the original model, picked 1,792 positions, and at each one forced each of the model's top four candidate tokens. Then I let it finish 16 times from each and checked whether its accuracy depended on the choice.

About **10%** of positions mattered, and they were overwhelmingly positions where the model was **nearly certain**: the next number in a calculation, the term being substituted. Where the model hesitates, between "Let's" and "We" or where to break a line, the options are interchangeable. The model's uncertainty points almost exactly away from the decisions that matter.

KL looks the other way: **85% of it comes from the 20% of positions where the model is least sure.** Those are mostly wording choices. That explains how distillation can lower KL without helping accuracy: it's easiest to reduce KL on exactly the positions that don't matter.

So the natural weighted KL is simple: **only count KL at positions where the original model is confident**, say where its top token has probability above 0.99.

## Why the obvious fix isn't enough

At first this looked like the answer. On distillation checkpoints, including 18 I trained after settling on it, confident-position KL ordered pairs of checkpoints by accuracy correctly 97% of the time, against 92% for plain KL.

But a proxy chosen on one set of models can fail on the next, so I built a test designed to break it. I generated 43 new quantization variants, using different number formats and quantizing different parts of the network. Without measuring any accuracy, I picked the 14 on which plain KL and confident-position KL disagreed most. Then I measured accuracy to see which was right.

<!--KL_TEST-->

Confident-position KL did worse than a coin flip. Where the two measures disagreed, it was right on only **5 of 40** pairs.

Looking at the failures showed why. In one variant, **99% of its confident-position KL came from 1% of positions**, a few formatting spots like the decimal point after `0`. There, the quantized model gave the original model's token almost no probability, so each such spot added around 10 units of KL, while a typical position adds almost nothing. But the model rarely acted on them: when it wrote its own solutions, it didn't commit to a wrong token there, and its accuracy barely moved.

Weighting fixed *where* KL looks, but not *what* it measures. Two problems remained, both visible in the lemma:

1. **KL's penalty per token is unbounded,** but one wrong token can at most fail one problem. A few extreme positions can swamp everything else.
2. **KL measures disagreement in probabilities,** but what costs accuracy is a token the quantized model actually *writes*, on *its own* path.

## Counting committed errors

The lemma says to follow the quantized model through its own solutions and add up the damage from the tokens it picks. We can't compute the damage exactly, but we can recognize the tokens that cause most of it. This gives a rule:

1. Have the quantized model write one solution per problem.
2. Run the original model over each solution to get its probability for every token.
3. Count the tokens where **the quantized model was confident** (probability above 0.3) and **the original model rules the token out** (probability below 0.1%).
4. Divide by the number of solutions. I call this the **confident-error rate**.

Each piece maps onto the lemma:

- **The quantized model's own solutions** are the states the lemma averages over.
- **"The original model rules it out"** picks out tokens with large negative advantage. At positions where the original model is confident, the alternatives are almost always worse.
- **Counting** gives each error a bounded cost, like a failed problem. Versions that add up log-probability ratios did no better than KL.
- **"The quantized model was confident"** separates real mistakes from noise. Low-confidence oddities are mostly harmless wording. Confident ones are mostly substantive: wrong numbers, wrong operations. They also persist. Resampling from the same point brings a confident wrong token back about three times in four, and a low-confidence one almost never.

To check that these tokens really cause failures, I took solutions containing one and resampled the rest of the solution twice: once keeping the token, once swapping in the original model's choice. On problems the original model always solves, for a checkpoint from the middle of a distillation run, keeping the token made failure about seven times more likely (25% against 3.5%).

## Does it work?

I fixed this rule before training the checkpoints it was later tested on, so those are a fair test. On the **32 checkpoints made afterwards**, it orders pairs by accuracy correctly **94%** of the time, against **90%** for KL. Where the two disagree, it's right on 26 of 40 pairs. On the test built to break confident-position KL, it ties plain KL at 88%. It's the only measure I tried that never did worse than plain KL on any group of checkpoints.

<!--KL_SCATTER-->

It's also not fragile. Moving the quantized-model threshold anywhere from 0.1 to 0.5, or the original-model threshold anywhere from 1% to 0.01%, still beats KL on the checkpoints outside that test. And it needs no answer key, no grader, and nothing specific to math. The one cost is that the quantized model has to write one solution per problem, which is still much cheaper than a full evaluation with many samples.

## What this means for distillation

QAD usually minimizes KL, and most KL sits on wording choices, so the loss can keep improving while the mistakes that matter barely move. In my runs this was clearest with aggressive training. At a high learning rate, accuracy dipped below the untrained starting point partway through training, even though KL kept falling. A gentler learning rate avoided the dip and recovered about three times as much accuracy by the end.

The confident-error rate isn't perfect here either: it misses part of that mid-training dip. I also tried training directly on confident-position KL, and it didn't beat ordinary KL training. For now the new measure is a way to evaluate, not a better loss.

## Takeaways

- **KL answers a different question from the one you care about.** It asks how different the predictions are on the original model's text. Accuracy depends on which mistakes the quantized model makes on its own.
- **Weighting KL toward important positions helps, but isn't enough.** A few extreme positions dominate it, and probability gaps aren't mistakes.
- **Count the mistakes directly:** confident tokens in the quantized model's own output that the original model rules out.

All of this comes from one model, on math, with weight-only quantization. The natural next step is to check that the rule carries over to other models and tasks.
